h: Hezekiah is the model of a king who trusts the LORD, even to the point of destroying a sacred object that had become an idol.
Faithfulness does not exempt God’s people from crisis, and buying peace from the world does not bring it.
The enemy’s strongest weapon is the argument that God cannot or will not save; the question of the chapter is whether the LORD is just another national god.
When God’s name is mocked, his people can bring the matter to him and leave the defence of his honour in his hands.
The conflict is no longer between two kings but between the king of Assyria and the God of Israel.
Faithful prayer starts with who God is, tells him the truth about the situation, and asks for help so that his name will be known.
The proud empire that thinks it controls history is only an instrument in God’s hand, and he will defend his people for his own name’s sake.
God delivers his people by his own power, and those who mock him come to nothing.
Even when God’s people lose, it is because God has handed them over, and he has not let go of them.
God’s people can serve inside a pagan system while drawing clear lines where obedience to God is at stake.
God, not Babylon, is the source of true wisdom, and his servant outlasts the empire that took him captive.
Human wisdom reaches its limit exactly where God’s revelation begins.
Daniel’s first response to answered prayer is praise, and his praise declares that God rules the times and the kings.
Every human empire, however glorious, is temporary; God’s kingdom, coming from outside human history, will fill the earth and last for ever.
God honours those who honour him, and makes even pagan kings acknowledge his power.
Empires demand worship; God’s people must decide in advance whom they will bow to.
Real faith says ‘he is able’ and ‘even if he does not’ in the same breath.
God does not always keep his people out of the fire, but he is with them in it.
The most powerful king of his age publicly confesses that God’s kingdom, not his, is everlasting.
Nebuchadnezzar’s Dream of a Great Tree
God sets kings up and brings them down, so that everyone may know who really rules.
A faithful servant speaks hard truth with compassion, and calls even the powerful to repent.
Pride that takes God’s glory for itself is brought low.
Sanity begins with looking up to God; the humbled king ends by praising the King of heaven.
Treating holy things with contempt is a sign of a heart and a kingdom ripe for judgment.
The arrogant feast is interrupted by a message no human wisdom can read.
Those who know the truth and still defy God are weighed and found wanting, and his judgment comes on time.
A life so blameless that enemies can attack it only through its faithfulness to God is the best witness.
Daniel’s courage lies in quiet, unchanged faithfulness, and God vindicates him.
The stories end where the visions will begin: God’s kingdom outlasts every empire.
Daniel’s Vision of the Four Beasts
From heaven’s point of view, the great empires of the world are beasts.
Daniel’s Vision of the Ancient of Days
Above the noise of the beasts, God sits enthroned as judge, and the outcome is decided in his court.
Daniel’s Vision of the Son of Man
God’s kingdom is given to one like a son of man, and Jesus claimed to be him.
God’s people may be persecuted for a limited time, but the kingdom will be theirs for ever.
Daniel’s Vision of the Ram and the Goat
Even the desecration of God’s sanctuary has a set limit, after which it will be restored.
God names the empires before they appear, and the most arrogant persecutor will be broken without a human hand.
True prayer takes God’s promises seriously, confesses sin honestly, and pleads God’s mercy and name rather than our merit.
Gabriel’s Prophecy of the Seventy Weeks
God’s plan reaches beyond the return from exile to a final dealing with sin, through an Anointed One who is cut off.
Prayer is heard from the first day, even when the answer is delayed by conflicts we cannot see.
Kings of the South and North
The rise and fall of the greatest empires was known to God before it happened.
The Wars of the Ptolemies and Seleucids
Kings scheme and fight, but the course of history is known to God in advance, down to its details.
Antiochus IV and the Abomination of Desolation
When faith is persecuted, those who know their God stand firm, and even their suffering refines them.
The final arrogant enemy of God, whoever he proves to be, comes to his end with no one to help him.
Beyond the worst distress lies resurrection: everlasting life for God’s people, and glory for those who lead others to righteousness.
We are not given every answer about the timing, but we are given a promise: rest, and then resurrection.
Jesus is the goal of Israel’s whole history: the King promised to David and the blessing promised to Abraham, and God brought him through outsiders and sinners as well as kings.
Jesus is God with us, conceived by the Holy Spirit without a human father, and he came to save his people from their sins.
Gentile seekers come a long way to worship the King of the Jews, while Israel’s king plots to kill him and its scholars know where he is, but Matthew records none of them going.
Jesus relives Israel’s story as the true and faithful Son; even as a refugee child he is under his Father’s care.
The coming of the King provokes violence against the innocent; God does not hide the grief, but sets it inside the story of his promised rescue.
God guides his Son’s family step by step, and even Jesus’ humble home town carries meaning.
The Mission of John the Baptist
No religious background can replace a changed life; the King is coming, bringing the Spirit to those who repent and judgment to those who refuse.
Jesus takes his place with sinners in obedience to the Father, and the Father and the Spirit publicly declare him the beloved Son and chosen Servant.
Jesus, the faithful Son, defeats the devil by trusting and obeying his Father where Israel failed; his victory is the hope of all who are tempted.
Jesus brings God’s light first to the dark, despised, mixed-up places, and calls everyone to turn to God because his kingdom has come near.
Jesus calls ordinary people to leave everything and follow him, and promises to make them into people who bring others to God.
Jesus’ teaching, preaching and healing show that God’s kingdom has arrived and give a preview of the world he will make new.
Jesus, the promised prophet greater than Moses, teaches those who follow him what life under God’s reign looks like, from the inside out.

God’s blessing rests not on the proud and successful but on those who know their need of him; their character is a picture of Jesus, and the kingdom of heaven is theirs now and fully in the age to come.
Jesus’ followers are salt and light: by being different, they hold back the world’s decay and show God’s goodness so that people praise him.
Jesus does not cancel the Old Testament; he fulfils it, and he calls his people to a righteousness of the heart that goes deeper than outward religion.
God judges anger and contempt, not only murder, so Jesus’ followers must hurry to make peace with those they have wronged.
Jesus says that lust in the heart is already adultery before God, and calls his followers to take drastic action against anything that leads them into sin.
Jesus restores God’s purpose for marriage as a lifelong covenant and protects the vulnerable from careless divorce.
Jesus’ followers should be so truthful that their plain ‘yes’ or ‘no’ can be trusted without any oath.
Jesus calls his followers to give up personal revenge, absorbing wrongs and returning good for evil, as he himself did.
God’s children are to love even their enemies, as their Father does, aiming at the complete, undivided love that reflects his character.
Do good deeds, including giving, for God’s eyes and not for applause; the Father who sees in secret will reward his children.
Prayer is not a performance for others or a technique to move God, but honest trust in a Father who sees in secret and knows what we need.
Jesus teaches us to pray as children to our Father: first for his name, kingdom and will, then for our daily bread, forgiveness and protection.
Fasting, like giving and prayer, is for God alone; done in secret, it expresses our hunger for him, and he rewards it.
Earthly wealth cannot last, so invest your life in what God values; your heart will follow your treasure.
A generous, undivided heart fills life with light; no one can serve both God and money, so we must choose whom we will serve.
Because our heavenly Father knows and cares for us, we can stop worrying, seek his kingdom first, and trust him for what we need, one day at a time.
Jesus forbids harsh, hypocritical judgement of others; deal humbly with your own faults first, then help others gently, and use wise discernment.
Keep asking, seeking and knocking, because your Father loves to give good gifts; and treat others as you would want to be treated, which sums up the Law and the Prophets.
Jesus calls everyone to choose: the easy, crowded road leads to destruction, but the narrow way of following him leads to life.
False teachers, and false disciples, are known by their fruit; on the last day what counts is not impressive words or deeds but being known by Jesus and doing the Father’s will.
Hearing Jesus’ words is not enough; only the one who acts on them builds a life that will stand on the day of judgement.
Jesus teaches with a unique, personal authority that astonishes the crowds; the right response is not only amazement but obedience.
Jesus is both able and willing to make the unclean clean; his touch does not make him unclean but brings healing and restores outcasts to God’s people.
Faith that trusts the authority of Jesus’ word is what God looks for, and people from every nation who trust him will share the feast of his kingdom.
Jesus is Isaiah’s suffering Servant, who takes up our sicknesses and sins; his healings preview the complete restoration his death will win.
Following Jesus means putting him before comfort, security and even the most sacred family duties, because he has the right to our first loyalty.
Jesus commands the wind and the sea as only God can; his disciples may face storms, but with him in the boat they need not be ruled by fear.
Jesus has complete authority over evil powers and can set its victims free with a word, yet people can still choose to send him away.
Jesus, the Son of Man, has authority on earth to forgive sins, and he proves it by healing a paralysed man; forgiveness is our deepest need.
Jesus calls the despised and the sinful to follow him and welcomes them to his table, because he came as a doctor for the sick, not for those who think they are well.
Jesus is the bridegroom whose presence brings joy; his coming is something new that cannot simply be patched onto the old, and his followers fast in longing while he is away.
Jesus’ touch cleanses the unclean and raises the dead; those who come to him in faith, however desperate, find him able to save.
Jesus Heals the Blind and Mute
Jesus, the Son of David, opens blind eyes and gives speech to the mute as the prophets promised; the same works lead some to faith and others to harden their hearts.
Jesus’ compassion for helpless people moves him to call his disciples to pray for workers, and then to send them out; the harvest is God’s and it is ready.
Jesus chooses twelve ordinary, very different men, gives them his authority and sends them out, gathering and renewing God’s people around himself.
Jesus sends his disciples to announce and show the kingdom, travelling light, giving freely and trusting God, while warning that rejecting the message is serious.
Jesus sends his disciples out vulnerable among hostile people, calling them to be wise and pure, promising the Spirit’s help and final salvation to those who endure.
Do not fear people: the truth will come out, God alone holds our eternal destiny, and he cares for us in every detail, so we can confess Jesus openly.
Jesus divides people because he demands first place, above family and life itself; those who lose their life for him find true life.
Jesus is present in his messengers, so welcoming them is welcoming him and his Father; no act of kindness to his people, however small, will go unrewarded.
When doubts come, Jesus points to his works, which fulfil the prophets’ promises; blessed are those who trust him even when he does not act as they expected.
John was the greatest of the prophets, the promised forerunner, yet the kingdom Jesus brings is greater still; people who will not respond to God find fault with every messenger.
The greater the light people have received, the greater their responsibility; seeing God at work and not repenting brings heavier judgement than the sins of pagan cities.
God reveals himself to the humble through his Son, who alone truly knows the Father; and Jesus invites all who are weary to come to him for rest.
Jesus is greater than the temple and Lord of the Sabbath; God gave the day of rest for mercy and blessing, not as a burden, and Jesus alone has authority to say what it means.
It is always right to do good on the Sabbath; Jesus restores a man’s hand, while those who put rules above mercy begin to plot his death.
Jesus is Isaiah’s gentle Servant, filled with God’s Spirit, who does not crush the weak but quietly brings justice and hope to the nations.
Jesus drives out demons by the Spirit of God, proving that God’s kingdom has come and that the stronger one has bound Satan; no one can stay neutral about him.
Every sin can be forgiven except the hardened refusal to recognise the Spirit’s work in Jesus; our words reveal our hearts and will be judged.
Jesus refuses signs to those who will not believe, but offers the sign of his death and resurrection; he is greater than Jonah and Solomon, so rejecting him is graver than any pagan’s unbelief.
Reform without new life leaves a person or people empty and in greater danger; the cleansed heart must be filled by God himself.
Jesus’ true family are those who do the will of his Father; everyone who follows him becomes his brother, sister or mother in the family of God.
The message of the kingdom meets different kinds of hearts; much seed seems wasted, but where it is received it produces an astonishing harvest.
Jesus’ parables reveal the secrets of the kingdom to those who come to him and hide them from those who have hardened their hearts; his disciples are blessed to see what prophets longed to see.
The Parable of the Sower Explained
The same word is heard by everyone; the devil, persecution and worldly cares can stop it bearing fruit, but those who truly hear and understand it produce a rich harvest.
God’s kingdom has come, yet evil still grows alongside it, sown by the enemy; God will separate the two at the harvest, so his servants must wait patiently for his judgement.
The Parable of the Mustard Seed
God’s kingdom begins as small as a mustard seed but grows into a great tree; what God plants will become far greater than its beginnings suggest.
Like a little leaven working through a great batch of dough, God’s kingdom works quietly and unseen until its influence spreads through everything.
I Will Open My Mouth in Parables
Matthew explains that Jesus’ parables fulfil Psalm 78: through them Jesus reveals what God had kept hidden from the beginning.
The Parable of the Weeds Explained
Jesus, the Son of Man, will judge the world at the end of the age, removing all evil and making the righteous shine like the sun in their Father’s kingdom.
The Parables of the Treasure and the Pearl
The kingdom of heaven is a treasure worth more than everything we have; those who truly see its worth gladly give up all to gain it.
At the end of the age God will separate the wicked from the righteous; disciples who understand Jesus become teachers who bring out treasures old and new.
Familiarity can blind people to who Jesus is; his own town took offence at him, and their unbelief kept them from seeing his mighty works.
John the Baptist was killed for speaking God’s truth to a powerful man; his death foreshadows the death of Jesus, and shows the cost of faithfulness.
The Feeding of the Five Thousand
Jesus, the compassionate Shepherd, feeds thousands from five loaves; he takes the little his disciples bring and makes it more than enough.
Jesus walks on the sea as only God can; when Peter looks away from him and sinks, Jesus saves him, and the disciples worship him as the Son of God.
Sick people throughout the region came to Jesus and were healed by touching the edge of his cloak; his power flowed freely to all who came to him in need.
Jesus condemns human traditions that cancel God’s commands, and worship that honours God with the lips while the heart is far from him.
Real uncleanness comes not from food or unwashed hands but from the human heart; only God can make the heart clean.
The Faith of the Canaanite Woman
A Gentile mother refuses to give up, trusting that even a crumb of Jesus’ grace is enough; he praises her great faith and heals her daughter.
The Feeding of the Four Thousand
Jesus heals many and feeds four thousand; the compassion he showed Israel reaches this crowd too, which may have been largely Gentile.
Jesus refuses to perform a sign on demand for those who will not believe; they can read the sky but not what God is doing, and the only sign they will get is his resurrection.
The Leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees
Jesus warns his disciples against the spreading influence of the Pharisees’ and Sadducees’ teaching, and rebukes them for forgetting how he has provided for them.
Peter, taught by the Father, confesses Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God, and Jesus promises to build his church, which nothing will overcome.
Jesus begins to teach that he must suffer, die and rise; when Peter tries to stop him, Jesus rebukes him for thinking in human terms instead of God’s.
To follow Jesus is to deny yourself and take up your cross; those who lose their lives for him will find true life when he returns in glory.
On the mountain three disciples see Jesus’ divine glory, Moses and Elijah bear witness to him, and the Father commands, ‘Listen to Him!’; the glorious Son must still go the way of suffering.
Coming down from the mountain, Jesus meets human misery and unbelief; where his disciples fail, he frees a tormented boy with a word.
The disciples failed because they did not truly trust Jesus; even faith as small as a mustard seed, placed in God, can do what seems impossible.
The Second Prediction of the Passion
Jesus again foretells that he will be handed over, killed and raised; God’s hand is behind the human hands, and the story does not end in death.
As God’s Son, Jesus is free from the temple tax, yet he pays it to avoid needless offence; he provides the coin in a fish’s mouth, showing his authority over all creation.
The way into the kingdom, and the way to greatness in it, is to humble yourself like a little child; Jesus counts the welcome given to his humble followers as given to him.
Jesus fiercely protects his humble followers, warning of judgement on anyone who causes them to fall, and calls every disciple to deal ruthlessly with whatever leads them into sin.
The Parable of the Lost Sheep
God so values each humble believer that he seeks the one who strays like a shepherd seeking a lost sheep; his people must never look down on the little ones but share his searching love.
When a brother sins, go to him privately, then with witnesses, then to the church, always aiming to win him back; the church’s faithful decisions carry heaven’s authority.
When believers gather in Jesus’ name, especially to seek wisdom in hard matters, the Father hears their united prayer and Jesus himself is present with them.
God has forgiven us a debt we could never pay; those who have received such mercy must forgive others from the heart, without keeping count.
God made marriage as a lifelong one-flesh union that no one should break; divorce was a concession to hard hearts, and singleness for the kingdom is also a gift.
Jesus welcomes and blesses the children his disciples tried to turn away; the kingdom belongs to those who come to him like children.
Eternal life cannot be earned by good deeds; Jesus exposes the rich young man’s love of wealth and calls him to give it up and follow him, but he goes away sad.
It is impossible for the rich, or anyone, to save themselves; but with God all things are possible, even freeing someone from the grip of wealth.
The Reward of Those Who Follow
Jesus promises that his apostles will share his rule in the renewed creation, and that everyone who gives up anything for him will receive far more and inherit eternal life.
God rewards his servants not by strict wages but by his generosity; those who come late receive the same grace, and no one should resent his goodness to others.
The Third Prediction of the Passion
For the third time Jesus foretells in detail that he will be condemned, mocked, flogged and crucified, and rise on the third day; he walks towards it willingly.
Two disciples seek the highest places in Jesus’ kingdom; he asks whether they can drink his cup of suffering, and teaches that the Father assigns honour in his kingdom.
In Jesus’ kingdom greatness means serving others, because the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many.
The Blind Men by the Road
Two blind men cry to Jesus, the Son of David, for mercy; he stops for them, opens their eyes in compassion, and they follow him.
Jesus enters Jerusalem as the gentle King of Zechariah’s prophecy, openly claiming his throne, though the city does not yet know who he is.
Jesus comes to the temple as its Lord, clearing out those who used it for gain and healing the needy, while children praise him and the leaders seethe.
The withered fig tree is a living parable of judgement on showy but fruitless religion, and Jesus turns it into a call to faith-filled prayer.
When the leaders question Jesus’ authority, his question about John exposes that they are not seeking truth but protecting their position.
The Parable of the Two Sons
Doing the Father’s will matters more than saying the right words; repentant sinners enter the kingdom ahead of religious people who never repent.
The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
Jesus tells the leaders, in a parable, that they are about to kill God’s Son as their fathers killed the prophets, but the rejected stone will become the cornerstone.
God’s invitation to his Son’s wedding feast goes out to all, good and bad, but those who come must be clothed for it; many are called, but few are chosen.
Jesus escapes the trap by giving Caesar his due coin and claiming for God the far greater thing that bears his image: ourselves.
Jesus answers the Sadducees from God’s power and from Moses himself: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob is the God of the living, so the resurrection is certain.
The whole law hangs on two inseparable commands: love God with everything you are, and love your neighbour as yourself.
With one question from Psalm 110, Jesus shows that the Messiah is not only David’s son but David’s Lord, enthroned at God’s right hand.
Jesus warns against leaders who teach but do not practise, load burdens on others and crave honour; his followers are brothers under one Father and one Teacher, and the greatest is the servant.
Jesus pronounces woes on leaders who block the way into the kingdom, make converts to their own blindness, and play games with oaths, as if God were not present.
Jesus condemns religion that fusses over small outward things while neglecting justice, mercy, faithfulness and a clean heart.
Those who honoured the dead prophets were about to kill God’s Son and his messengers, filling up their fathers’ sins; judgement would fall on that generation.

Jesus grieves over Jerusalem like a mother hen whose chicks will not come; the temple is left desolate, and the city will not see him again until it says, ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.’
Jesus foretells the temple’s destruction and warns his disciples not to be deceived or alarmed by false messiahs, wars and disasters, which are only the beginning of birth pains.
Jesus warns of persecution, betrayal, false prophets and cooling love, but promises that those who endure will be saved and the gospel will reach all nations.
Jesus warns his followers to flee without delay when they see the abomination Daniel foretold, promises that God will shorten the days of great distress, and guards them against false messiahs.
The Return of the Son of Man
The Son of Man’s coming will be as unmistakable as lightning, not a rumour to chase; he comes with power and great glory and gathers his elect from the four winds.
The Lesson of the Fig Tree
As fig leaves signal summer, the signs Jesus gave would show that what he foretold was near; heaven and earth will pass away, but his words never will.
No one knows the day of Christ’s return, not even the Son on earth, so his followers must live ready at every hour, unlike Noah’s generation.
The faithful servant keeps caring for the household until the master returns; the one who thinks ‘My master will be away a long time’ abuses others and is judged as a hypocrite.
The Parable of the Ten Virgins
The bridegroom came later than expected; those who were ready went in, and the door was shut on those who were not, so keep watch.
Christ has entrusted his servants with his possessions; the faithful use them and share their master’s joy, while the servant who buried his talent out of a false view of his master is cast out.
The Son of Man will judge the nations as King, welcoming those whose love for the least of his brothers showed they were his, and sending away those who neglected him in them.
Jesus foretells that he will be handed over to be crucified at Passover, while the leaders secretly plot to kill him after the feast.
A woman pours costly perfume on Jesus, and he defends her ‘waste’ as a beautiful act that prepares his body for burial and will be remembered wherever the gospel is preached.
Judas, one of the Twelve, offers to hand Jesus over to the chief priests and agrees to do it for thirty pieces of silver.
Jesus, knowing that his time has come, sends his disciples to prepare the Passover meal at a house he has chosen.
At the meal at Passover time Jesus announces that one of the Twelve will betray him, declaring that his death fulfils Scripture yet pronouncing woe on the betrayer.

At the meal at Passover time Jesus gives bread and wine as his body and his blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins, and looks forward to drinking it new in his Father’s kingdom.
Jesus warns that all the disciples will fall away as Scripture foretold, and that Peter will deny him three times, but promises to go ahead of them to Galilee after he rises.
In anguish Jesus prays for the cup to pass from him, yet submits to his Father’s will, while his disciples sleep instead of keeping watch.
Judas betrays Jesus with a kiss; Jesus forbids his disciples to defend him with the sword, freely gives himself up to fulfil the Scriptures, and all the disciples flee.

Before the council Jesus stays silent against false witnesses, then declares under oath that he is the Christ and the Son of Man who will sit at God’s right hand, and is condemned for blasphemy and mocked.
Peter, warming himself in the high priest’s courtyard, denies three times that he knows Jesus, then hears the rooster crow, remembers Jesus’ words and weeps bitterly.
Judas, seized with remorse, returns the silver and hangs himself, and the priests buy a potter’s field with the blood money, fulfilling what the prophets foretold.
Before Pilate Jesus acknowledges that he is the King of the Jews but makes no reply to the leaders’ accusations, leaving the governor amazed.
Offered a choice, the crowd demands the release of Barabbas and the crucifixion of Jesus; Pilate, though he knows Jesus is innocent, washes his hands and hands him over to be crucified.
The true King is crowned with thorns.
Jesus stays on the cross precisely in order to save others.
Jesus’ death opens the way to God, shakes creation, and breaks the power of death itself.
Jesus was truly dead and buried, in a known tomb watched by witnesses.
Jesus’ enemies remembered his promise to rise better than his friends did, and their precautions became evidence for the empty tomb.
Jesus has risen as he said; the first witnesses were women, and the risen Lord calls his failed disciples ‘My brothers’.
The earliest explanation from Jesus’ opponents admits that the tomb was empty.
The risen Jesus has all authority, sends his church to make disciples of every nation, and promises his presence to the end: Immanuel, God with us (1:23).
The Mission of John the Baptist
The Father, the Son and the Spirit all appear at the start of the gospel, and the ‘Lord’ whose way Isaiah said would be prepared turns out to be Jesus.
The Temptation and Preaching of Jesus
The long-awaited reign of God has arrived in Jesus, and the right response is to turn round and trust the good news.
Following Jesus starts with his call, and it costs something real.
Jesus’ authority is not borrowed from earlier teachers; evil itself recognises and obeys him.
Jesus brings God’s healing right into an ordinary home, and the healed woman responds by serving.
Jesus’ priorities came from time alone with his Father, not from the demands of the crowd.
Jesus is both able and willing, and his touch reverses contamination: holiness flows outward from him.
Jesus claims to do what only God can do, and proves it with something everyone can see.
Jesus seeks out the people religious society wrote off; only those who know they are sick come to the doctor.
Jesus’ presence is a time for joy; his followers would fast after he was taken away.
The kingdom Jesus brings is not a patch on the old system but something new.
The Sabbath is God’s gift, and Jesus is its Lord.
Refusing to do good is itself a choice for evil; and Jesus’ anger at hard hearts is mixed with grief.
Jesus did not accept testimony to himself from demons; he would make himself known in his own way and time.
Jesus chooses unlikely people, wants them first to be with him, and then sends them out.
Jesus’ exorcisms are not Satan’s tricks but Satan’s defeat.
Every sin can be forgiven, except the settled refusal that calls God’s saving work evil and so shuts the door on the only source of forgiveness.
Jesus’ followers become his family, closer even than blood.
Much of the sowing seems wasted, but the harvest will be astonishing.
The same word that opens the eyes of seekers leaves the indifferent more blind.
The Parable of the Sower Explained
What matters is not a quick, joyful start but lasting fruit; and the threats are Satan, suffering and the cares and riches of life.
Those who listen carefully receive more; those who ignore what they have heard lose even that.
The sower sows, but God gives the growth, quietly, steadily and beyond our understanding, until the harvest.
The Parable of the Mustard Seed
From a Galilean teacher and twelve followers, the kingdom of God will grow beyond all expectation.
The one asleep in the boat is the Lord who stills the sea (Psalm 107:28–29), and his presence is the answer to fear.
No one is too far gone for Jesus; and the first missionary to the Gentile Decapolis is a man who had been possessed by a legion.
Jesus has time for the outcast and power over death; for him, death is like sleep from which he wakes people.
Familiarity with Jesus’ ordinary life became, for his own town, a reason not to believe.
Jesus shares his mission and his authority with his followers, and sends them out dependent on God.
A weak man who knew what was right chose to save face; and the forerunner’s death foreshadows what awaits Jesus.
The Feeding of the Five Thousand
Jesus is the shepherd Israel lacked (Ezekiel 34), who feeds his people in the wilderness as God fed them with manna.
Jesus does what only God does and speaks as God speaks; yet even his closest followers were slow to understand.
Where people come to Jesus with their need, he does not turn them away.
Religious rules can become a way of avoiding what God actually commands.
Our real problem is not outside us but inside; and Christ’s coming ends the food laws that once marked Israel off.
The Faith of the Gentile Woman
God’s blessing came to Israel first, but a Gentile mother’s humble, persistent faith shows it was always meant for the nations too.
Jesus does the works Isaiah said would mark God’s coming, and he deals with each person in a way they can understand.
The Feeding of the Four Thousand
Jesus’ compassion and provision reach Gentiles as well as Jews.
Jesus does not perform on demand for people who have already decided not to believe.
The Leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod
Unbelief can be catching; and even disciples can be slow to see what is in front of them.
A two-stage healing, placed where Mark puts it, pictures the disciples: they see something of Jesus, but not yet clearly.
Everything turns on the question every reader must answer: ‘Who do you say I am?’
The Christ must suffer, die and rise; any version of him without the cross is the devil’s idea.
Following a crucified Messiah means dying to self; but that is the only way to find life.
For a moment the disciples see the glory hidden in Jesus, and the Father tells them to listen to him, above Moses and Elijah.
The Boy with an Evil Spirit
Jesus welcomes weak, mixed faith that turns to him; and his followers’ power depends on dependence on God in prayer.
The Second Prediction of the Passion
Jesus kept telling them plainly; they did not want to hear.
Greatness in Jesus’ kingdom is measured by service to the least important; and his people should not be jealous of others working in his name.
Sin is so deadly that nothing is too precious to give up in order to avoid it; Jesus means the urgency, not literal self-harm.
Disciples will be refined by trial; they must keep their distinctive savour and live at peace.
Marriage is God’s work, joining a man and a woman as one for life; divorce is a concession to sin, not God’s design.
The kingdom is received, not earned, by the dependent and the small, and Jesus has time for children.
No one can earn eternal life; salvation is impossible for us and possible only for God, and anything we hold onto above Jesus must go.
The Third Prediction of the Passion
Jesus walked towards his death with open eyes and set purpose.
